title: Conditionals & Advanced
subtitle: The Crossroads of If
intro: At the Crossroads of If, every path is a possibility: real, imagined, or lost in the past. Here you'll also learn to report what others said, connect ideas with who and which, and avoid the double-negative trap.

rules.title: Zero & First Conditionals

story.line: Hana reaches a crossroads. A glowing crystal ball floats in the air.
If you heat ice, it melts. That is always true. We call it the zero conditional: if + present, present.
And if I study hard, I will pass the test!
That's the first conditional: a real possibility in the future. If + present, will + verb.
If I will win, I will be famous!
No will in the if-part! 'If I win, I will be famous.'

parts.name: Zero conditional
parts.detail: General truths. If + present, present.
parts.example: If you mix red and blue, you get purple.

parts.name: First conditional
parts.detail: Likely future. If + present, will + base verb.
parts.example: If it rains, we will stay home.

parts.name: No will after if
parts.detail: Use present tense in the if-clause.
parts.example: If she calls, I'll answer. (not If she will call)

parts.name: Comma rule
parts.detail: Comma when the if-clause comes first; none when it comes second.
parts.example: We'll stay home if it rains.

parts.name: Unless = if not
parts.detail: A handy variation.
parts.example: Unless you hurry, you'll miss the train.

rules.history:
Conditionals in English are built from ordinary tenses rather than special endings. The rule 'no will in the if-clause' comes from the fact that will originally meant 'want': 'If you will come' once meant 'if you are willing to come.'

That older meaning still survives in polite phrases like 'If you will follow me, please,' which is why it's not totally wrong, just special.

examples.good: If I see Yumi, I'll tell her.
examples.bad: If I will see Yumi, I'll tell her.

examples.good: Plants die if they don't get water.
Unless you apologize, she won't forgive you.

rules.trick: If is a gate. Will can't pass through the gate; it waits on the other side.

quiz.q: 'If it ___ tomorrow, we'll cancel the picnic.'

rules.title: Second Conditional
rules.tagline: Imaginary present or future: If I were...

story.line: If I had a dragon, I would ride it to school every day.
But you don't have a dragon.
That's exactly why he uses the second conditional: an imaginary or unlikely situation. If + past simple, would + verb.
If I were the queen, I would ban homework! Hehe.
Notice: Yumi said 'If I were,' not 'If I was.' That's the subjunctive, used for unreal situations.

parts.name: Form
parts.detail: If + past simple, would / could / might + base verb.
parts.example: If I won the lottery, I would travel.

parts.name: Meaning
parts.detail: Unreal now, or very unlikely in the future.
parts.example: If I had wings, I could fly.

parts.name: Were for everyone
parts.detail: In careful English, use were with all subjects.
parts.example: If he were taller, he'd play basketball.

parts.name: Advice
parts.detail: If I were you...
parts.example: If I were you, I'd apologize.

rules.history:
Using a past tense to talk about an imaginary present seems strange, but many languages do it. Linguists call it 'remoteness': the past form pushes the idea further away from reality, just as it pushes events further back in time.

The 'were' form is a survivor of the Old English subjunctive mood, which once had its own set of endings.

examples.good: If I knew her number, I would call her.
examples.bad: If I would know her number, I would call her.

examples.good: If I were rich, I'd buy a castle.
What would you do if you saw a ghost?

rules.trick: Second conditional = daydream mode. Past tense in the dream (if I had...), would in the result.

quiz.q: 'If I ___ more time, I would learn the guitar.'

quiz.why: would + base verb in the result.

rules.title: Third Conditional
rules.tagline: Regrets about the past: If I had known...

story.line: Kaito stares at a burnt cake.
If I had set a timer, I would have saved the cake...
The third conditional: an imaginary past that didn't happen. If + had + past participle, would have + past participle.
It's the grammar of regret!
If you had asked me, I would have eaten it before it burned. Hehe.

parts.name: Form
parts.detail: If + had + past participle, would have + past participle.
parts.example: If I had studied, I would have passed.

parts.name: Meaning
parts.detail: The past can't change; we imagine a different version.
parts.example: If we had left earlier, we wouldn't have missed the bus.

parts.name: Could / might have
parts.detail: Other modals work too.
parts.example: If she had trained, she might have won.

parts.name: Mixed conditional
parts.detail: Past condition, present result.
parts.example: If I had taken the job, I would be rich now.

rules.history:
This form stacks the past perfect inside the if-clause with 'would have' in the result. It's one of the most complex structures in everyday English.

In casual speech, people often say 'If I would have known,' especially in American English. It's common in speech, but teachers and editors still treat it as incorrect in writing.

examples.good: If you had told me, I would have helped.
examples.bad: If you would have told me, I would have helped.

examples.good: She wouldn't have been late if she had woken up on time.
If I had saved money, I would be on vacation now.

rules.trick: Regret = HAD in the if, WOULD HAVE in the result. 'If I had... I would have...'

quiz.q: 'If I ___ the alarm, I wouldn't have overslept.'
'If she had practiced, she ___ the contest.'

rules.title: Reported Speech

story.line: Sensei said, “I am tired.”
How do I report that without the quotes?
Shift everything one step back in time: 'Sensei said that he was tired.' Am becomes was. I becomes he.
And if I said, “I will win tomorrow”?
Kaito said that he would win the next day. Will → would. Tomorrow → the next day.

parts.name: Backshift tenses
parts.detail: Move one step into the past.
parts.example: am → was, will → would, can → could, have done → had done

parts.name: Change pronouns
parts.detail: From the reporter's point of view.
parts.example: “I love you” → She said she loved me.

parts.name: Change time & place words
parts.detail: now → then, today → that day, here → there.
parts.example: “I'm here now” → He said he was there then.

parts.name: Reported questions
parts.detail: Use if/whether or the question word, and normal word order.
parts.example: “Are you OK?” → She asked if I was OK.

parts.name: No backshift needed
parts.detail: When it's still true.
parts.example: He said the earth is round.

rules.history:
Backshifting is called 'sequence of tenses' and it follows a logic found in Latin and many European languages: the reported words are placed in the time frame of the reporting verb.

Modern English is more relaxed than Latin. If the statement is still true or very recent, many speakers don't backshift at all: 'She said she's coming.'

examples.good: He said he was hungry.
examples.note: No quotation marks in reported speech.

examples.good: She asked where I lived.
examples.bad: She asked where did I live.
examples.note: Reported questions use normal word order.

examples.good: They told me they would call.
examples.bad: They told me they will call.
examples.note: Will → would (unless still in the future).

rules.trick: Reporting is time travel: step the verb back one floor in Chrono's tower.

quiz.q: “I can swim.” → She said she ___ swim.

quiz.why: Normal word order in reported questions.

rules.title: Relative Clauses: Who, Which, That

story.line: The sword that Kaito found is magic.
'That Kaito found' tells us which sword. It's essential, so no commas.
My sword, which I found in a cave, is magic!
That 'which' clause is extra information. Remove it and we still know which sword. Extra info = commas + which.
And for people, use who! 'The kitsune who stole the sword is very cute.' Hehe.

parts.name: Who
parts.detail: For people.
parts.example: The girl who won is my friend.

parts.name: Which
parts.detail: For things and animals, especially extra info with commas.
parts.example: My bike, which is red, was stolen.

parts.name: That
parts.detail: For things (and people informally) in essential clauses, no commas.
parts.example: The bike that I bought is red.

parts.name: Essential vs. extra
parts.detail: Essential = identifies which one (no commas). Extra = bonus info (commas).
parts.example: My brother who lives in Paris (I have several) vs. My brother, who lives in Paris, (I have one)

parts.name: Whose, where, when
parts.detail: Possession, place, time.
parts.example: the man whose car broke, the town where I grew up

rules.history:
Who and which come from Old English question words (hwā, hwilc). That was originally a form of 'the.' For centuries writers used which and that interchangeably (the King James Bible says 'Our Father, which art in heaven').

In 1926, H. W. Fowler's 'A Dictionary of Modern English Usage' suggested using that for essential clauses and which for extra ones. American editors adopted his suggestion strongly; British writers are more relaxed and often use which for both.

examples.good: The movie that we watched was scary.
examples.bad: The movie, that we watched, was scary.
examples.note: Don't put commas around a that-clause.

examples.good: Tokyo, which is huge, never sleeps.
examples.bad: Tokyo that is huge never sleeps.
examples.note: There's only one Tokyo, so the info is extra.

examples.good: The teacher who helped me retired.
examples.bad: The teacher which helped me retired.

rules.trick: Which = a bonus scene (with comma curtains). That = part of the main plot (no curtains).

quiz.q: 'Mount Fuji, ___ is Japan's highest mountain, is beautiful.'

rules.title: Double Negatives

story.line: I didn't eat nothing!
So you ate something! Hehe. Two negatives make a positive!
That's not what I meant!
In standard English, use one negative: 'I didn't eat anything' or 'I ate nothing.'
But songs say 'I can't get no satisfaction'!
Many dialects and songs use double negatives for emphasis, and everyone understands them. In formal writing, though, one negative is the rule.

parts.name: Negative words
parts.detail: not / n't, no, never, nothing, nobody, nowhere, none, neither.
parts.example: I never lie.

parts.name: Use any- after not
parts.detail: anything, anybody, anywhere, any, ever.
parts.example: I don't know anybody here.

parts.name: Hidden negatives
parts.detail: hardly, barely, scarcely are already negative.
parts.example: I can hardly see. (not can't hardly)

parts.name: Litotes (on purpose)
parts.detail: 'Not un-' for gentle meaning is fine.
parts.example: It's not unusual. (= it's fairly common)

rules.history:
In Old and Middle English, double and even triple negatives were normal and simply made the 'no' stronger. Chaucer famously described a knight who 'never yet no villainy ne said / in all his life unto no manner wight': four negatives in two lines!

In the 1700s, grammarians such as Robert Lowth (1762) declared that two negatives cancel each other out, borrowing logic from mathematics and Latin. Their rule became standard in schools, while many spoken dialects kept the older style.

examples.good: I don't have any money.
Nobody ever tells me anything.
I can hardly wait.

rules.trick: One 'no' per idea. After a negative, switch to 'any' words.

rules.title: Question Tags

story.line: You love me, don't you, Kaito?
Why are you asking me a question at the end of a sentence?
That's a question tag. A tiny question attached to a statement, to check or invite agreement.
Positive sentence, negative tag. Negative sentence, positive tag. 'It's cold, isn't it?' 'You aren't scared, are you?'
And the tag copies the helper verb. If there's no helper, use do, does or did.

parts.name: Opposite polarity
parts.detail: Positive → negative tag; negative → positive tag.
parts.example: She's nice, isn't she? / He can't swim, can he?

parts.name: Copy the helper
parts.detail: be, have, modals, or do.
parts.example: You've finished, haven't you?

parts.name: No helper? Use do
parts.detail: Match the tense.
parts.example: You like tea, don't you? / He went, didn't he?

parts.name: Special cases
parts.detail: I am → aren't I? / Let's → shall we?
parts.example: I'm late, aren't I? Let's go, shall we?

rules.history:
Tags like 'is it not?' already appear in Shakespeare's plays. As contractions spread in the 1600s and 1700s, they shrank into the quick forms we use today, like 'isn't it?'

Many languages have a single simple tag, like Japanese 'ne?', French 'n'est-ce pas?' or German 'oder?'. English is unusual because its tags change to match each sentence's verb, which makes them tricky but very expressive.

examples.good: It's a beautiful day, isn't it?
examples.bad: It's a beautiful day, is it?

examples.good: You don't like spiders, do you?
examples.bad: You don't like spiders, don't you?

examples.good: She plays tennis, doesn't she?

rules.trick: Tags are mirrors: they flip positive and negative, and copy the helper verb.
